notes.meaning: Jephthah was a brave and skilled fighter, but he grew up with the shame of being born to a prostitute. His father was a man named Gilead from the tribe of Manasseh, who lived east of the Jordan River. God often chooses to work through people who come from broken family backgrounds.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that Gilead here may refer to the leader of the Gilead clan rather than Jephthah's literal father.

notes.meaning: When Gilead's wife had sons who grew up, they drove Jephthah away from his home. They told him he would receive no family inheritance because his mother was another woman. Their harsh treatment revealed deep personal hatred alongside their legal arguments.

Jephthah fled from his brothers and settled in the land of Tob, outside Israel's borders. Landless and desperate men gathered around him, and he became the commander of a band of raiders. Jephthah trained these men well and used them to protect the frontier from surrounding enemies.

Some time later, the army of Ammon invaded the land and attacked Israel. The elders of Gilead had no skilled general, so they traveled to Tob to bring Jephthah back. They asked him to serve as their military commander to fight the Ammonites.

Jephthah reminded the leaders that they had hated him and allowed him to be chased from his father's house. He asked why they were turning to him only now when they were in deep trouble. The elders admitted their past wrong and offered to make him the permanent ruler of all Gilead if he led them to battle.

Jephthah asked for a clear commitment before agreeing to fight. He wanted to know if they would truly keep him as ruler once the Lord gave him victory over the Ammonites. The elders swore a solemn oath before the Lord that they would do everything he said.

Jephthah returned with the elders, and the gathered assembly of Gilead formally confirmed him as their leader and general. At the town of Mizpah, Jephthah repeated the terms of the agreement before the Lord. He placed his new authority and mission directly under God's watchful care.

Jephthah sent messengers to the king of Ammon to ask why he was invading Israel's land. The Ammonite king claimed that Israel had stolen his territory between the Arnon and Jabbok rivers during the Exodus and demanded it back. Jephthah wisely sought a peaceful solution through honest discussion before going to war.

Jephthah sent envoys back to the king to correct his false claim. He stated clearly that Israel had never taken any land that belonged to Ammon or Moab. A wise leader speaks the truth plainly to avoid unnecessary bloodshed.

Jephthah reviewed the historical journey of Israel after leaving Egypt and traveling to Kadesh. When the kings of Edom and Moab refused to let Israel cross their borders, Israel peacefully went around their territories. They set up camp north of the Arnon River, respecting the river as Moab's actual border.

Israel sent messengers to Sihon, the Amorite king ruling in Heshbon, asking for safe passage through his territory. Sihon distrusted Israel and refused to grant permission. Instead, he gathered his army at Jahaz and attacked Israel without any provocation.

The Lord gave Sihon and all his forces into Israel's hands, and Israel defeated them. As a result, Israel took possession of all the land belonging to the Amorites. This territory reached from the Arnon to the Jabbok River, and from the eastern desert to the Jordan River.

Jephthah pointed out that the Lord had driven out the Amorites, not the Ammonites, so Ammon had no rightful claim to the land. He noted that the Ammonites would keep whatever territory their god Chemosh gave them. In the same way, Israel would hold on to whatever land the Lord their God had granted them.

Jephthah asked if the king thought he was better than Balak, the ancient king of Moab, who never attempted to wage war to take this land back. Israel had lived peacefully in Heshbon, Aroer, and nearby towns for three hundred years without dispute. Such a long period of quiet possession proved that Ammon's sudden claim was unlawful.

Jephthah declared that Israel had committed no sin against Ammon, but Ammon was doing wrong by starting a war. He asked the Lord, the ultimate Judge of all people, to decide between the two nations. The king of Ammon refused to listen to Jephthah's message, making battle unavoidable.

The Spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah, giving him unusual courage, wisdom, and leadership. He traveled through Gilead and Manasseh to rally the Israelite forces and gather them at Mizpah. God equips His servants with the spiritual power they need to carry out His work.

differ.view: Some Reformed commentators argue that because the Spirit came upon Jephthah here, his subsequent vow was made under the Spirit's guidance rather than in foolishness.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view this verse as an editorial link connecting the earlier diplomatic messages to the war story.

notes.meaning: Before going into battle, Jephthah made a solemn promise to God in order to secure a victory. He vowed that whatever came out of the doors of his house to meet him on his return would belong to the Lord as a burnt offering, a gift burned on an altar. God never asked for such a careless bargain, which risked offering a person in direct violation of God's law.

differ.view: Jephthah intended to offer a human being as a literal sacrifice, influenced by surrounding pagan customs.
Jephthah intended either an animal sacrifice or the lifelong dedication of a person to God's service.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The vow was foolish and sinful, reflecting pagan influences rather than true devotion to God.

notes.meaning: Jephthah marched out to battle, and the Lord handed the Ammonites over to him. He struck down twenty of their towns with a crushing blow, completely subduing their forces. The victory was God's gracious gift to Israel, not the result of Jephthah's impulsive vow.

When Jephthah returned home to Mizpah, his daughter came out first to meet him with music and joyful dancing. She was his only child, and he had no other son or daughter to carry on his family name. A moment of great celebration suddenly turned into terrible sorrow.

As soon as Jephthah saw her, he tore his clothes in grief and cried out that she had brought him to his knees. He felt bound by his spoken vow and believed he had no way to turn back. Sadly, Jephthah did not realize that God's law forbade human sacrifice and provided ways to redeem unlawful vows.

differ.view: Many Reformed teachers believe Jephthah should have broken his rash vow and repented, because keeping a vow that harms someone is worse than breaking it.

notes.meaning: Jephthah's daughter answered with remarkable love and obedience toward her father and the Lord. She urged him to keep his word, since God had fully delivered the nation from the Ammonites. Her attitude showed deep personal faith and respect for her country's rescue.

She asked for two months to wander the hills with her friends and weep because she would never marry. In ancient Israel, remaining unmarried and childless was considered a very heavy loss and disgrace. Her father granted her request, and she spent the two months with her companions on the mountains.

After two months, she returned home, and her father carried out the vow he had made. The passage emphasizes that she lived and died without ever having known a man intimately. This tragic event became a lasting custom and remembrance throughout Israel.

differ.view: Jephthah carried out an actual human sacrifice, showing how deeply Israel had fallen into lawlessness and moral decay.
Jephthah dedicated his daughter to lifelong celibacy and service at the tabernacle rather than putting her to death.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early Christian tradition and the plain text indicate that Jephthah actually sacrificed his daughter out of misguided zeal.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The Hebrew statement about her virginity describes her status at the time she was put to death rather than a lifetime of celibacy.

notes.meaning: Each year, the young women of Israel set apart four days to remember and honor the daughter of Jephthah. Her courage and willing sacrifice left a permanent mark on the nation's memory. Remembering such moments reminded the people of the great cost of thoughtless words.
